newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Slaying of U.S. businessman alarms Moscow expats.
newsitem.headline: Slaying of U.S. businessman alarms Moscow expats.

text.p: The street murder of a prominent U.S. businessman involved in a multi-million-dollar local real estate dispute sent shivers of fear through Moscow's foreign business community on Monday.
An unknown assailant gunned down Paul Tatum, a flamboyant and maverick businessman, with a Kalashnikov sub-machinegun outside the Kievskaya metro station on Sunday afternoon.

Tatum fell metres (yards) from the Radisson-Slavjanskaya luxury hotel, U.S. President Bill Clinton's favourite Moscow residence, over which Tatum was locked in lawsuits which he said were worth about $50 million.
American Chamber of Commerce executive director Peter Charow said on Monday the killing, the first of a U.S. businessman since Russia's free-market explosion, was a turning point.
"The fact that that line has been crossed has got to give people pause. We (foreigners) didn't think we were immune, but history has been on our side," he said.
"This message is going to be picked up in the boardrooms back in the States," Charow said.

Russia, once one of the safest countries in the world, has seen crime rates jump since economic and political reforms began five years ago, and Moscow residents have become used to street violence, often between rival gangs.

The U.S. embassy, which had advised its citizens on Friday to be cautious this week during expected demonstrations, said it "deplores this violent murder" and was waiting for further details of the shooting.
Tatum died in hospital.
A Russian woman near the metro when Tatum was shot said she fled after what she thought was a normal gangster affair.
"I thought it was a normal shooting between Russian businessmen," she said when a long burst of gunfire blasted through the underground pedestrian tunnel into which Tatum fell.
Foreign businessmen in Moscow had mixed opinions whether their community would begin packing its bags and heading home.
Stephen Kuzara, General Manager of computer firm Acer Inc CIS, said his executives were already leery of Russia.

Acer decided not to build a computer assembly plant in Russia because of its poor business infrastructure, and Kuzara said he had dropped plans for a legal action against a Russian competitor after he was threatened.

"All foreign businessmen have to make a decision whether to cross the unwritten line. Paul Tatum had more to lose and a bigger investment. He didn't have much support from the legal infrastructure -- the result speaks for itself."

Tatum, a 39-year-old Oklahoma City native, according to associates, had been fighting a legal battle with Moscow city authorities over control of the Radisson-Slavjanskaya, which opened in 1991. He lived in a suite in the disputed hotel.

He had run advertisements in local papers to publicise his situation and sought public financial support in "freedom bonds" to pay for his court cases in the Stockholm arbitration court, which executives at Tatum's company, Americom, said they were winning.
Police have not reported any suspects in the killing, though they described the attempt, and a sub-machinegun left in a plastic bag near the murder spot, as evidence of a contract hit.
But some saddened expatriates said Tatum's death would have little effect on the community.
"Paul was aggressive and flamboyant enough so that not too many people saw themselves in him," said a foreign stockbroker living in Moscow, adding that Western investment would continue.
Last year as he fought to get back into his Radisson offices, Tatum, effectively prophesied his own end in an interview with the British newspaper The Independent.
"I'm here till they carry me out," he said.
